nameStory: The spoonleaf sundew gets its name from its distinctive spoon-shaped leaves that widen at the tip, quite different from the perfectly round leaves of its cousin, the round-leaved sundew. The 'sundew' part comes from the glistening droplets of sticky 'dew' that coat the leaves, sparkling like diamonds in the sunlight. This isn't actually dew at all, but a clever trap for catching tiny insects!
description: Spoonleaf sundew is a tiny carnivorous plant that looks like it belongs in a fairy garden. The entire plant is only about 2-4 inches tall, forming a small rosette of reddish-green leaves that are wider at the tip than at the base, giving them their characteristic spoon shape. Each leaf is covered in tiny red tentacles tipped with sparkling droplets of sticky fluid that trap small insects. In summer, it sends up delicate white or pinkish flowers on thin stems that rise above the leaves.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Spoon-shaped leaves that are narrow at the base and widen toward the tip, covered in red tentacles with sticky, glistening droplets that feel tacky to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a tiny rosette close to the ground, usually 2-4 inches across, often growing in small clusters or mats

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white or pale pink flowers on thin, wiry stems that rise 4-6 inches above the leaves, blooming from June through August

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaves feel slightly succulent and the sticky droplets are noticeably tacky if you gently touch them (though it's best to avoid touching)

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Reddish-green to bright red coloration, especially intense in sunny locations, with the red tentacles creating a fuzzy appearance

habitat: Look for spoonleaf sundew in acidic, nutrient-poor wetlands like sphagnum bogs, wet sandy shores of ponds and lakes, and the edges of cranberry bogs. It thrives in constantly moist to wet soils that stay soggy year-round, often growing alongside sphagnum moss, pitcher plants, and bog cranberry. You'll find it in both full sun and partial shade, from sea level to moderate elevations throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green, gradually developing their red coloration and sticky tentacles as the weather warms. The plant forms its characteristic rosette shape.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with fully developed spoon-shaped leaves covered in glistening droplets. White or pink flowers appear on thin stems from June through August.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may become more intensely red before dying back. Seeds ripen and disperse from the dried flower stalks.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to underground roots and dormant buds, completely disappearing above ground until spring returns.

funFact: This tiny plant is actually a skilled predator that can digest an entire small fly in just a few days, dissolving it with enzymes similar to those in your stomach to absorb nutrients that are missing from bog soils!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with round-leaved sundew, but spoonleaf sundew has leaves that are clearly wider at the tip (like a spoon), while round-leaved sundew has perfectly circular leaves on long stems. Memory trick: 'Spoon-shaped for spoonleaf, round for round-leaved' – the names match the shapes!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being carnivorous, sundews are completely harmless to humans – the sticky traps are only strong enough to catch tiny insects like gnats and mosquitoes. The plant supplements poor bog nutrition by 'eating' bugs, making it one of nature's most specialized bog dwellers.
compareHints: Spoonleaf sundew differs from round-leaved sundew by its spoon-shaped leaves (versus perfectly round) and its tendency to grow in wetter areas. Thread-leaved sundew, found mainly in coastal areas, has long, thin, thread-like leaves rather than the broad spoon shape. All three species share the characteristic sticky, glistening tentacles that make sundews unmistakable.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Round-leaved sundew differs from spoonleaf sundew by its perfectly circular leaves (versus oval spoon-shaped ones) and typically grows in more open bog areas.
Unlike its sundew relatives, thread-leaved sundew has long, thin, upright leaves rather than the round, flat leaves of round-leaved sundew or the spoon-shaped leaves of spoonleaf sundew.
